cards.title: A budget is a plan, not a punishment
cards.body: A budget just means deciding where your money goes before it disappears. Every dollar gets a job: spend, save, or invest. Dollars with no job vanish on impulse buys.

cards.title: The 50/30/20 rule
cards.body: Split take-home pay into 50% needs (rent, groceries, transport), 30% wants (eating out, hobbies), and 20% savings plus debt payoff. It's a starting template, not a law — adjust the dials to your life.
Maya takes home $2,400 a month. Needs: $1,200 (rent $900, groceries $200, bus pass $100). Wants: $720. Future: $480 straight to savings. Every dollar has an address.
Track every dollar for 30 days before judging yourself. Most people find 10–15% leaking to forgotten subscriptions and snacks. You can't fix what you can't see.

cards.q: You take home $3,000/month. Under 50/30/20, how much goes to savings?
cards.explain: 20% of $3,000 = $600. That's the pay-yourself-first slice — needs get $1,500, wants get $900.

flashcards.back: 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings and debt payoff — a starter template for splitting take-home pay.
Needs keep life running: rent, food, transport. Wants make it fun: dining out, games. The line moves per person — be honest with yourself.
Move savings out the moment you're paid, before spending. What you don't see, you won't miss.
To find the leaks — forgotten subscriptions and impulse buys most people underestimate by 10–15%.

questions.q: Needs now eat 60% of your pay after a rent hike. What do you do?
choices: Put rent on a credit card
questions.explain: Ratios are guides, not cages. When needs swell, shrink wants first and protect at least some savings.

questions.q: Which of these is a need?
choices: Bus pass to get to work
New sneakers when the old ones are fine
questions.explain: If skipping it breaks your ability to live or work, it's a need. Everything else is a want — even fun, legitimate ones.

questions.q: You find $200/month in forgotten subscriptions. Best move?
choices: Cancel them and redirect it to savings
Find new subscriptions to replace them
questions.explain: $200 a month is $2,400 a year. Redirecting found money to savings is the highest-return 'raise' you'll ever give yourself.

choices: They're unrealistic and abandoned by week two
questions.explain: Brutal, joyless budgets die fast. Build in guilt-free fun money and the plan survives.

cards.title: Pay yourself first, automatically
cards.body: Willpower is unreliable; automation isn't. Set a transfer that moves money to savings the day you're paid. You adapt to what's left, and saving happens whether you feel like it or not.

cards.title: Kill high-interest debt first
cards.body: Credit card debt at 20%+ grows faster than any safe investment earns. The avalanche method: pay minimums everywhere, then throw every extra dollar at the highest-rate balance first.

$3,000 on a card at 22% with $60 minimum payments takes 7+ years and costs about $2,800 in interest. Paying $200/month clears it in 18 months for about $550 in interest. Same debt, $2,250 difference — from the payment size alone.
Build a $500–$1,000 mini emergency fund before attacking debt aggressively. Without it, every car repair lands right back on the card and you're running in circles.

cards.q: Two debts: $800 at 24% and $2,000 at 8%. Avalanche says attack which first?
cards.explain: Avalanche targets the highest rate first — 24% costs far more per dollar than 8%, regardless of balance size.

flashcards.back: Pay minimums on all debts, send every extra dollar to the highest-interest balance first. The mathematically cheapest way out.
Willpower fades; automatic transfers happen regardless. You spend what's left instead of saving what's left.

flashcards.front: What is an emergency fund for?
flashcards.back: Surprise expenses — repairs, job loss — so they don't land on high-interest credit cards.

flashcards.front: Why are minimum payments a trap?
flashcards.back: They're calibrated to stretch repayment for years, maximizing the interest you pay.

questions.q: $500 extra this month. Card A: $1,200 at 21%. Card B: $900 at 12%. Avalanche says?
questions.explain: Highest rate first, always, under avalanche. Card A's 21% bleeds faster per dollar than Card B's 12%.

questions.q: What's a reasonable starter emergency fund?
choices: $0 — the credit card IS the fund
questions.explain: A small buffer breaks the borrow-for-emergencies cycle. Grow it to 3–6 months of expenses later.

questions.q: Savings earn 4%, your card charges 22%. Extra $1,000 goes…
questions.explain: A 22% guaranteed 'return' from killing debt crushes 4% savings interest. Pay the expensive debt first.

questions.q: What happens if you only ever pay minimums?
choices: You pay far more interest over far more years
The debt vanishes at the same speed
Your credit score instantly maxes out
questions.explain: Minimums are calibrated to keep you paying mostly interest. Bigger payments attack principal.

questions.q: Best day for the automatic savings transfer?
choices: Payday — before you can spend it
End of month, if anything's left
Never — do it manually when inspired
questions.explain: Pay yourself first means first. End-of-month leftovers are a myth, and inspiration is unreliable.

cards.title: Compound interest is a snowball
cards.body: Returns earn returns. $200 a month at roughly 7% average annual growth means $24,000 contributed over 10 years becomes about $34,000 in value — the extra $10,000 is growth earning its own growth.

cards.title: Stocks vs. bonds in one breath
cards.body: Stocks are tiny ownership slices of companies — higher growth, bumpier ride. Bonds are IOUs that pay steady interest — calmer, slower. Young investors usually lean toward stocks; the mix gets calmer with age.

Two friends invest $5,000 once at 7% average. Ana starts at 25, Ben at 35. At 65: Ana has about $74,000, Ben about $38,000. Same money, same return — ten extra years nearly doubled the outcome. Time is the real asset.

Index funds bundle hundreds of stocks into one cheap package — instant diversification without picking winners. Low fees matter more than clever picks: a 1% fee can eat a third of your returns over decades.

cards.q: Why do low fees matter so much?
choices: They compound against you for decades
They only apply to rich investors
cards.explain: A 1% annual fee sounds small, but over 30+ years it can devour roughly a third of your total gains. Fees compound too — against you.

flashcards.back: Earning returns on your returns — growth that snowballs because each year's gains start earning too.
One fund holding hundreds of stocks: instant diversification at very low fees.
Stocks = company ownership, higher growth, more volatility. Bonds = loans paying steady interest, calmer and slower.
Time amplifies compounding. Small amounts invested young can outgrow larger amounts started late.

questions.q: What does diversification protect you from?
questions.explain: Spreading across many holdings means one flop can't sink you. It can't remove market-wide risk — just single-company risk.

questions.q: $1,000 at 10% for a year, then the $1,100 compounds another year at 10%. Total?
questions.explain: Year 1: $1,100. Year 2: 10% of $1,100 = $110, total $1,210. That extra $10 is interest earning interest.

questions.q: Which typically has the highest long-term returns?
questions.explain: Stocks have historically returned around 7–10% annually over long periods — with plenty of scary dips along the way.

questions.q: A fund charges 1.5% yearly vs. a similar one at 0.1%. Over 30 years…
choices: The expensive one can cost roughly a third of your gains
The expensive one must perform better
questions.explain: Fees compound relentlessly. Higher fees don't buy higher returns — they just guarantee a bigger cut for the fund.

questions.q: Best first investing move for a beginner?
choices: A low-fee diversified index fund, held long-term
Betting everything on one hot stock tip
questions.explain: Boring wins: diversify cheaply, keep buying, don't panic-sell. Stock tips and market timing are how beginners donate money.
